lines.say: Play a piano chord. How does your ear pick out the notes?
One tangled wave arrives, yet you hear three separate notes.
Your ear splits that wave into frequencies, how fast each note vibrates. That's a Fourier transform.
The quantum Fourier transform, or Q F T, does the same to amplitudes, the numbers that set each reading's chance when you measure.
Two qubits, quantum bits, have four possible readings, zero to three.
Put equal amplitudes on zero and two, leaving one and three empty. That pattern repeats every two steps.
Now run the Q F T, and the chance peaks at frequencies zero and two.
Here's why. Each input sends every output a clock hand, and where it points is its phase.
From zero, every hand points up. From two, each turns half a circle more than the last.
At outputs one and three, up cancels down, while at zero and two they add. That's interference.
Slide the pattern onto one and three, and the peaks stay put. The Q F T hears the rhythm, wherever it starts.
Here the chord picture breaks. Your ear hears every note at once.
But measuring gives one frequency per run, picked at random from the peaks.
That's no good for listing every note in your data, but plenty when you need one hidden rhythm.
Shor's algorithm finds one, and uses it to break huge numbers into their factors.
So the Q F T turns rhythm into position.
With N readings, a pattern repeating every r steps lands on multiples of N over r.
